newsitem.title: USA: USDA opposes bills to deregulate futures markets.
newsitem.headline: USDA opposes bills to deregulate futures markets.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Tuesday he opposed proposed legislation before Congress that would deregulate the futures exchanges.
"I believe regulatory policy must continue its present balance," Glickman said in a letter dated May 5 to Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairwoman Brooksley Born.

"Before I would support changing it, I would want to be assured that the changes would not jeopardize the public function of the exchange markets in the interest of enhancing their profit functions," the Agriculture Secretary wrote.

Glickman had specific reservations about a key provision, the so-called "pro-market exemption", saying: "I question whether it might increase the probability of price manipulation or fraud by reducing the indicators available to the Commission to detect such activity."
He also said he was concerned that the professional market could drain business from the remaining, more regulated markets, thus weakening them for retail investors.

The pro-market exemption would exclude certain transactions by professional traders from federal regulations. Proponents argue it is needed to cut regulatory costs for certain traders so they can better compete with the over-the-counter market.

"While I appreciate that point of view, I believe the effort to level the playing field between OTC and the exchange markets cannot be fully evaulated without examining the public benefits of regulation," Glickman wrote.

The CFTC has criticized the proposed legislation, which is pending before both the House and Senate, as stripping it of the tools it needs to prevent and detect fraud and manipulation in the futures and options markets.
The biggest U.S. futures exchanges have pressed Congress to rein in the CFTC's powers, saying the agency's paperwork and regulatory requirements make U.S. exchanges uncompetitive in a global market.
